summary: SCReAM is a rate adaptation algorithm for conversational media such as interactive video. It follows the packet conservation principle and uses hybrid loss-and-delay-based congestion control. It was evaluated in simulations and tests. This memo is Experimental.

eli5.summary: It adjusts how much video to send so a video call stays smooth without clogging the network when it gets crowded.

subtitle: Real-time rate adaptation for interactive video using self-clocked congestion control.

tldr.problem: Interactive video calls need to adapt their bitrate to changing network conditions without adding delay to the video, which is difficult when network capacity can change rapidly (especially over wireless).
tldr.mechanism: SCReAM uses a congestion window (like TCP) that grows and shrinks based on measured queuing delay, paired with a media rate control that adjusts the video encoder's bitrate based on both network state and the size of the send queue.
tldr.outcome: Video calls remain smooth and responsive, adjusting bitrate within one round-trip time of congestion detection, working across wired and wireless networks including LTE.

today: RFC 8298 is Experimental. SCReAM is implemented in WebRTC clients and real-world video applications, and continues to be tested and refined. It is not obsoleted by a standards-track successor, though ongoing research explores variants and improvements.

sections.title: The Real-Time Media Problem
sections.content: Unlike file downloads, interactive video calls must adapt their bitrate on the fly to the available network capacity. On wireless networks like LTE, the capacity can change dramatically in seconds due to radio quality, handovers, or network load. A traditional congestion control algorithm that reacts by waiting for packet loss is too slow: by the time loss arrives, the receive buffer has filled with packets, adding seconds of delay to the video. Interactive video cannot tolerate seconds of delay without breaking the conversation. SCReAM (Self-Clocked Rate Adaptation for Multimedia) combines ideas from TCP with real-time media requirements: self-clocking for fast, fine-grained rate control, delay-based congestion detection for responsiveness, and media rate control that prevents the send queue from filling up.
sections.eli5: Video calls need to be quick. File downloads can wait, but if a video call is slow, people can't hear each other. SCReAM notices congestion by how long packets are waiting, not by losing them.

sections.title: Three-Part Design: CWND, Media Rate, and Feedback
sections.content: SCReAM has three main pieces. First, a network congestion control that maintains a congestion window (CWND), limiting how many bytes can be in flight at once, similar to TCP. The CWND grows when the network is not congested (measured by queuing delay) and shrinks when loss or Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) occurs. Second, media rate control that adjusts the target bitrate for the video encoder, based on both the CWND and the size of the RTP send queue. If the queue builds up (packets waiting to be sent), the media bitrate is reduced; if the queue is empty, bitrate can increase. Third, a simple receiver that sends back RTCP feedback listing which packets arrived, the arrival time of the latest packet, and the count of ECN-marked packets. The sender uses this feedback to compute queuing delay and manage CWND.
sections.eli5: Three parts work together: one manages the network bottleneck (how much data can be in flight), one adjusts the video quality, and one sends status reports back so the sender knows what's happening.

sections.title: Congestion Window: Self-Clocking with Delay Detection
sections.content: SCReAM uses a self-clocked approach: it sends packets at a rate limited by the receiver's ability to acknowledge them, similar to TCP. The congestion window (CWND) puts a limit on bytes in flight. CWND grows if the queuing delay stays below a target (typically 50-100 milliseconds), using a technique similar to LEDBAT. The queuing delay (qdelay) is measured from RTP timestamps: the difference between when a packet was sent and when it was received, as reported in RTCP feedback. A key feature is the qdelay trend: even before the delay reaches the target, if it is trending upward or downward, SCReAM detects incipient congestion and slows down. CWND is also reduced when loss or ECN events occur. In fast increase mode (used at startup), CWND grows aggressively; after congestion is detected, it grows slowly based on the delay-to-target relationship. This dual-mode approach lets video calls ramp up quickly when the network is idle, then maintain stability under congestion.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps count of how much data is flying through the network. It's allowed to send more if things are moving fast (low delay), and must send less if things are backing up. Packets arriving back tell the sender if there's a queue building.

sections.title: Media Rate Control: Encoder Feedback
sections.content: The CWND limits total bytes in flight, but the video encoder produces frames at a variable bitrate (talking heads use little bitrate; scene changes use more). SCReAM manages an RTP packet send queue holding encoded frames waiting to be transmitted. The media rate control adjusts the video encoder's target bitrate based on two inputs: the CWND-based network state, and the size of the RTP queue. If the RTP queue is too large, packets are waiting to be sent, indicating the encoder is producing faster than the network can carry; the encoder bitrate is reduced. The algorithm uses a target_bitrate that the encoder should not exceed. In fast increase mode, the bitrate increases at a configured ramp-up speed (e.g., 200 kbps/s), letting it reach a useful quality within 5-10 seconds. In normal mode, bitrate increases based on the measured network throughput (from ACKs) and is limited by a guard factor that reduces jitter. When loss or ECN marks occur, the bitrate is immediately reduced. This separation of network control (CWND) from media control (encoder bitrate) makes it easy to extend SCReAM to multiple video streams: each stream has its own rate control, but they share a single CWND.
sections.eli5: The video encoder is told how much bitrate it's allowed to use. The encoder doesn't know about the network; it just listens to the rate control telling it to make video easier or harder depending on whether the send queue is empty or full.

sections.title: Competing Flows and Feedback
sections.content:
When SCReAM competes with loss-based flows (like TCP or FTP), it must adapt. Loss-based algorithms probe until packets drop, then back off sharply. If SCReAM's delay-based CWND stays low while loss-based flows push the queue to its limit, the loss-based traffic fills the buffer. SCReAM detects this by watching for loss events and high variance in delay measurements. If detected, it increases its delay target, allowing its CWND to grow more and compete for capacity. This trade-off is imperfect: increasing the delay target also increases end-to-end latency. But without it, SCReAM would starve against aggressive TCP flows.

The receiver side is minimal: for each RTP packet, it records arrival time and notes which packets are missing. Via RTCP, it sends a list of received packet sequence numbers (using Loss RLE encoding), the timestamp of the highest-sequence packet, and an ECN-marked packet count. SCReAM recommends frequent feedback (every 20-100 ms depending on bitrate) so that self-clocking works well. The sender reconstructs the loss pattern and derives the queuing delay from packet timestamps.
sections.eli5: If a greedy file-transfer hogs the queue, SCReAM detects it and allows itself a little more delay so it's not starved out. The receiver just tells the sender which packets arrived and when, and the sender figures out what to do.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 8298 is Experimental. SCReAM has been implemented in WebRTC clients (OpenWebRTC) and is included in some real deployments. It was designed for mobile interactive video but works over any network. The algorithm requires compatible RTP/RTCP feedback, which is a standard part of WebRTC. An important constraint is that sender and receiver clocks must have the same frequency (though they do not need to be synchronized) for accurate delay measurement; if clocks drift, qdelay calculation will be wrong.

Further experiments are encouraged on different access technologies (Wi-Fi, DSL, 5G), with various media types, under different competing traffic scenarios, and with refined parameters for edge cases like very low or very high bitrates. The default parameters (RAMP_UP_SPEED, TARGET delays, gain factors) are chosen from extensive testing with H.264 and VP8 video codecs, but may need tuning for specialized use cases. Security depends on RTCP feedback integrity: malicious modification of feedback or dropped RTCP packets can deceive the sender. Recommended countermeasures include RTCP integrity protection and a minimum send rate that survives temporary feedback loss.
sections.eli5: SCReAM is experimental and used in real WebRTC apps. The main risk is if the clock ticks at different speeds on sender and receiver, or if feedback packets get attacked. But it works well in practice for video calls.
